chapters.file: ch05 - Introduction.md
chapters.relation: Simon Riches's introduction frames the whole volume around Cronenberg's obsession with the Cartesian mind-body split, quoting the director that horror comes from being unable to reconcile a sharp mind with a dying body. It surveys the three parts of the book, showing how films like The Fly stage bodily transformation and personal identity, eXistenZ stages skepticism about the external world, and A History of Violence stages the nature of the self, arguing Cronenberg wears his philosophical interests 'on his sleeve.'

chapters.file: ch06 - Part 1. Body Horror and Bodily Transformation.md
ch07 - The Fly and the Human Ironies of Disgust.md
chapters.relation: Colin McGinn reads Cronenberg's The Fly as a meditation on human disgust and self-disgust: Seth Brundle's metamorphosis into Brundlefly does not cross an ontological boundary but dramatizes that the human being was already a loathsome organic monster, a 'god who shits.' McGinn ties this to a Cartesian mind-body duality (a fine mind trapped in a decaying insect shell mirrors our own embodiment) and, via Nussbaum, to how projected self-disgust stigmatizes despised groups; the cinematic image itself is an 'antidisgust medium' that lets us feel only quasi-disgust.

chapters.file: ch08 - Tragedy and Terrible Beauty in A History of Violence and Eastern Promises.md
chapters.relation: Cynthia Freeland argues A History of Violence and Eastern Promises qualify as Aristotelian tragedies, using the Poetics' 'recognition and reversal' as Tom Stall is exposed as Joey Cusack and Nikolai's undercover identity is revealed. Analyzing the stairway sex scene, the Philadelphia gunfight, and Nikolai's naked bathhouse fight, she deploys Korsmeyer's notion of 'terrible beauty' (beauty in the horrific, like the bloody newborn) and Carroll/Gaut on empathy and identification, concluding both heroes commit an Aristotelian hamartia through their acceptance of violence.

chapters.file: ch09 - Cronenberg as Scientist Antiessentialism, Sex as Remixing, and the View from Nowhere.md
chapters.relation: Peter Ludlow argues Cronenberg's true horror is scientific antiessentialism: The Fly, Shivers, Videodrome, and eXistenZ collapse the supposedly essential boundaries between human and fly, organic and mechanical, real and virtual, sane and mad, good and evil. Drawing on Quine's rejection of essence, Kripke's empirical essentialism, and Darwinian biology, he reads Brundle's fusion and Renn's VCR-stomach as showing we have no essence; sex is 'remixing' of information to lock out parasites, and Cronenberg narrates from Nagel's impersonal 'view from nowhere' where humans are not special.

chapters.file: ch10 - What Happens to Brundle Problems of Teleportation and Personal Identity in the Fly.md
chapters.relation: Paul Snowdon uses The Fly to press the metaphysics of teleportation and personal identity, asking whether the object leaving the first pod is identical to the one arriving or merely a replica (the reduplication problem). Adopting animalism, he argues Brundle likely ceases to exist at first teleportation, and that the fly-Brundle fusion is a new creature rather than Brundle, so Quaife's belief she is euthanizing Brundle is unsupported; a Lockean memory-based view (via Parfit) could vindicate her, but the audience's 'blind acceptance' of it gives that theory no evidential support.

chapters.file: ch11 - Part 2. Psychology, Skepticism, and the Self.md
ch12 - eXistenZial Angst.md
chapters.relation: Duncan Pritchard reads eXistenZ as staging radical skepticism with existential force: unlike the standard brain-in-a-vat scenario, the game 'creeps up' on Ted and Allegra so they feel the transition from reality to doubt, producing angst. Invoking Wittgenstein's On Certainty (doubt radicalized is madness), he argues sanity requires belief but not true belief, so the pair achieve a new doxastic equilibrium. He also reads the spinal 'bioport' pod as a case of Clark and Chalmers's extended cognition, where technology becomes part of and subverts the agents' cognitive processes.

chapters.file: ch13 - “Freaks of Nature” Extrasensory Perception and the Paranormal in the Films of David Cronenberg.md
chapters.relation: Keith Allen uses Stereo, Scanners, and The Dead Zone to explore the philosophy of ESP: telepathy and precognition challenge C. D. Broad's 'basic limiting principles' about causation (action at a distance, backward causation, changing the future). He asks whether ESP has the phenomenal 'tang' of genuine perception (Hume on force/vivacity; Nagel's 'what it is like'), and uses BonJour's reliable-clairvoyant Norman case plus Gettier to argue about internalist justification and knowledge, asking whether Johnny Smith needs reasons to trust his precognitive visions.

chapters.file: ch14 - Deception and Disorder Unraveling Cronenberg's Divided Minds.md
chapters.relation: Simon Riches traces Cronenberg's shift from bodily 'body horror' madness to psychological unraveling, focusing on Tom Stall's oscillation between Tom and Joey in A History of Violence. He treats self-deception via Davidson's 'divided minds' and Dennett's narrative-self view of multiple personality, situates hallucination (Spider, Videodrome) between Cartesian deception and psychosis, and uses Foucault, Kuhn, Szasz, and social constructionism to argue the category of mental disorder is socially contingent, so the line between self-deception and delusion (and mental order and disorder) is unclear.

chapters.file: ch15 - Psychological Determinism in the Films of David Cronenberg.md
chapters.relation: Daniel Shaw argues Cronenberg's oeuvre embodies psychological determinism (in Skinner's and Freudian terms), reading Dead Ringers as his masterpiece: Beverly Mantle's drug-fueled disintegration and murder of Elliot flow from an ambivalence and symbiotic bond he cannot escape, analyzed through Freud's Little Hans conflict of ambivalence and dream-as-wish. Surveying Shivers, The Brood, The Fly, and Crash as portraits of characters helplessly driven by parasites, disease, instinct, or trauma, he holds Eastern Promises (with its in-control hero Nikolai) is the pointed exception that proves Cronenberg's pessimistic determinist rule.

chapters.file: ch16 - Self-Creation, Identity, and Authenticity A Study of A History of Violence and Eastern Promises.md
chapters.relation: Daniel Moseley distinguishes metaphysical from practical problems of personal identity, arguing A History of Violence and Eastern Promises explore the practical: who Tom/Joey and Nikolai really are, as a matter of self-creation and self-discovery of a 'practical identity' (Korsgaard). Using Sartre's bad faith and Cavell on movie-star 'individualities,' plus Charles Taylor's critique of individualist authenticity, he argues even the wicked Semyon exemplifies authenticity, so authenticity is not a moral ideal, and Nikolai's decent double life may be worth being less authentic.

chapters.file: ch17 - Part 3. Words and Worldviews.md
ch18 - The Fiction of Truth in Fiction Some Reflections on Semantics and eXistenZ.md
chapters.relation: Graham Stevens uses eXistenZ to attack David Lewis's possible-world semantics for truth in fiction. Lewis analyzes 'according to the fiction f, p' as truth in the world(s) where the story is told as known fact; but eXistenZ's nested game-within-a-game ending, where even the characters cannot tell whether 'we are still in the game,' deliberately has no determinate world in which its events are fact. Stevens concludes fictions need not correspond to complete determinate worlds and proposes a stringent view: nothing is true in a fiction unless the fiction explicitly asserts it.

chapters.file: ch19 - Re(ct)ifying Empty Speech Cronenberg and the Problem of the First Person.md
chapters.relation: Brook W. R. Pearson examines the problem of the first person 'I' in Cronenberg through Lacan, Wittgenstein, and Deleuze/Guattari. He reads Spider's 'schizo-phonetic partition' and Tom/Joey's shifting use of 'I' in A History of Violence as Lacanian 'empty speech' and the narcissistic 'monument' of a censored unconscious chapter that resurfaces; Wittgenstein's private-language argument and Moore's paradox recast Joey's split as an illegitimate private language game, and Deleuze/Guattari's account of the other as a 'possible world' reframes the frightened face on the cinema screen.

chapters.file: ch20 - The Politics of Mad Science in The Fly and Dead Ringers.md
chapters.relation: R. Barton Palmer reads The Fly and Dead Ringers as a diptych on 'mad science' descended from Stevenson's Jekyll and Hyde rather than Frankenstein, in which the scientist turns the investigative gaze on himself and self-destructs. He grounds this in the Frankfurt School critique of Enlightenment (Adorno and Horkheimer's Dialectic of Enlightenment, Bacon's domination of nature, Marcuse's Eros and Civilization): Brundle's telepod and the Mantle twins' surgery expose the failure of Baconian objectivity and rationalization, with monstrousness emerging from within the divided self.

chapters.file: ch21 - From “Impassioned Morality” to “Bloodless Agnosticism” A Philosophy of David Cronenberg through the Burroughs.md
chapters.relation: Jones Irwin analyzes Cronenberg's adaptations of Burroughs's Naked Lunch and Ballard's Crash, arguing that while all three share an aesthetic of body horror and a Nietzschean perspectivist experimentalism, Burroughs and Ballard hold an 'impassioned moralism' (Crash as cautionary tale, Marcuse's one-dimensional man, an ethics of complicity and responsibility) that Cronenberg replaces with 'bloodless agnosticism.' Cronenberg aestheticizes Burroughs's wife-killing and reads Crash literally, using Plato's appearance/reality (cave) distinction to show he strips out the sociopolitical and moral frame the writers intended.
